column9: How many years after the Bohr Model was the Electron Cloud Model proposed?
column28: The Bohr Model was 1913 and the Electron Cloud Model was 1926. 1926 − 1913 = 13 years.
column29: Recall both years, then subtract the earlier year from the later one.

column9: Democritus had the idea of the atom around 400 BC, but the first atomic model was not proposed until Dalton in 1803. What was missing from Democritus's idea?
column28: Democritus used reasoning only. Science needs evidence from experiments, and later scientists gathered that evidence to build and test atomic models.
column29: What does every model after Democritus have that his idea did not?

column9: Thomson and Rutherford proposed their atomic models only a few years apart. Exactly how many years apart were they?
column28: The Plum Pudding Model was 1904 and the Nuclear Model was 1911. 1911 − 1904 = 7 years.
column29: Recall the year of each model, then subtract.

column9: Which atomic model lasted the SHORTEST time before the next model changed it?
column28: Solid Sphere lasted 1803–1904 (101 years), Plum Pudding 1904–1911 (7 years), Nuclear 1911–1913 (2 years), and Bohr 1913–1926 (13 years). The Nuclear Model was changed after only 2 years.
column29: Subtract the year of each model from the year of the model that came next.

column9: New experiments build on old ideas. Which scientist could have used Bohr's idea of fixed orbits when building his own model?
column28: Only a scientist who came after 1913 could build on Bohr's idea. Schrödinger's work led to the Electron Cloud Model in 1926. Rutherford (1911), Thomson (1904), and Dalton (1803) all came before Bohr.
column29: Which scientist on the list worked AFTER Bohr?

column9: Why was Moseley's way of ordering the periodic table an improvement on Mendeleev's?
column14: Each element has a unique atomic number, so ordering by protons puts every element in its correct place
column15: Atomic numbers were easier to measure in 1869
column16: Moseley used more decimal places in the atomic masses
column17: Moseley put the elements in alphabetical order
column28: Each element has a unique number of protons (atomic number), so ordering by atomic number puts every element in its own correct place. Ordering by atomic mass sometimes puts elements out of order.
column29: Which number identifies an element: its mass or its number of protons?

column9: Which ideas from older models are still part of the Electron Cloud Model? Select all that apply.
column14: The atom is divisible into smaller particles
column15: There is a small, dense, positive nucleus
column17: The atom is a solid sphere that can't get any smaller
column18: The positive charge is spread throughout the whole atom
column28: The Electron Cloud Model keeps Thomson's idea that the atom is divisible and Rutherford's small, dense, positive nucleus. It drops Bohr's fixed orbits, Dalton's solid sphere, and Thomson's spread-out positive charge.
column29: For each idea, ask: did any later model throw it out?

column9: How many years passed between Dalton's Solid Sphere Model and the Bohr Model?
column28: The Solid Sphere Model was 1803 and the Bohr Model was 1913. 1913 − 1803 = 110 years.
column29: Recall both years, then subtract the earlier one from the later one.

column9: Jae draws a positive nucleus with 6 electrons scattered around it, with no rings or paths. He labels it "Bohr Model." What should he change to make it a Bohr Model?
column15: Draw the electrons on fixed rings (orbits) around the nucleus
column16: Spread the positive charge through the whole atom
column17: Nothing; it is already a Bohr Model
column28: The Bohr Model puts electrons on fixed orbits (rings) around the nucleus. Jae's drawing, with a nucleus and electrons but no paths, matches Rutherford's Nuclear Model.
column29: What did Bohr add to Rutherford's model?

column9: Why didn't Thomson's 1904 model include a nucleus?
column14: Thomson thought atoms were solid spheres with nothing inside
column15: The cathode ray tube destroyed the nucleus
column16: The evidence for a nucleus, the gold foil experiment, had not been found yet
column17: Democritus had already proven atoms have no nucleus
column28: Models change when new evidence appears. The gold foil experiment that revealed the nucleus did not happen until 1911, so Thomson had no evidence of a dense center.
column29: When was the experiment that discovered the nucleus?

column9: Which pair of scientists did their work the FARTHEST apart in time?
column28: Democritus (about 400 BC) and Dalton (1803) are more than 2,000 years apart. Dalton and Thomson are 101 years apart, Thomson and Rutherford 7, and Bohr and Schrödinger 13.
column29: One pair crosses from ancient Greece to the 1800s.

column9: Rutherford fired positive particles at gold foil. Imagine the nucleus had been NEGATIVE instead. What would have happened to particles passing close to it?
column14: They would bounce straight back even more often
column17: They would be pulled toward the nucleus instead of pushed away
column28: Opposite charges attract, so positive particles would be pulled toward a negative nucleus instead of being pushed away. Particles bouncing back means the real nucleus is positive, like the particles.
column29: Do opposite charges attract or repel?

column9: Which result of the gold foil experiment would ALSO have happened if Thomson's Plum Pudding Model had been correct?
column15: A few particles bounced almost straight back
column16: Some particles were deflected at large angles
column17: Particles bounced back from a tiny, dense spot
column28: With positive charge spread thinly through the atom, particles would still pass straight through, so that result fits both models. Only the small, dense nucleus explains particles bouncing back or being deflected.
column29: Which result does NOT need a small, dense center to explain it?

column9: A scientist is writing a book in 1920. Which of these could NOT be in the book yet?
column28: In 1920 the gold foil experiment (1911), Moseley's atomic numbers (1913), and the Bohr Model (1913) were already known. The Electron Cloud Model was not proposed until 1926.
column29: Find the year of each one. Which happened after 1920?

column9: Ava says, "Dalton's model was useless, because it was wrong." Which response is best?
column14: She is right; a wrong model teaches scientists nothing.
column15: She is wrong; Dalton's model was wrong about atoms being unbreakable, but later models built on his idea that matter is made of atoms.
column16: She is wrong; Dalton's model is the one we still use today.
column17: She is right; Dalton did no experiments, like Democritus.
column28: Dalton was wrong that atoms can't be divided, but his model explained that matter is made of atoms and that compounds are atoms of different elements combined. Later models built on those ideas.
column29: Did later scientists keep any part of Dalton's model?

column9: Which model fits ALL of these clues? (1) The atom has a small, dense, positive center. (2) Electrons are found in shells around it. (3) An electron's exact path can't be predicted.
column28: Clue 1 rules out the Solid Sphere and Plum Pudding Models. Clue 2 rules out the Nuclear Model, which said nothing about shells. Clue 3 rules out Bohr's fixed orbits. Only the Electron Cloud Model fits all three.
column29: Use each clue to cross out models one at a time.

column9: Which statements about the Bohr Model are true? Select all that apply.
column14: Electrons travel in fixed orbits around the nucleus
column16: It was proposed the same year Moseley arranged the table by atomic number
column17: It was the first model with a nucleus
column18: It says electrons have no fixed paths
column28: Bohr's 1913 model kept Rutherford's nucleus and gave electrons fixed orbits, the same year Moseley arranged the periodic table by atomic number. The Nuclear Model (1911) was the first with a nucleus, and the Electron Cloud Model is the one with no fixed paths.
column29: Check each statement against the timeline, including the year.

column9: Put these discoveries and models in the order they happened, starting with the oldest.
column17: Mendeleev makes the first periodic table
column18: The Electron Cloud Model is proposed
column19: The cathode ray tube shows negative particles in atoms
column28: Mendeleev's periodic table (1869), cathode ray evidence for negative particles (1904), the gold foil experiment (1911), Bohr's fixed orbits (1913), the Electron Cloud Model (1926), and Chadwick's neutron (1932).
column29: Start with the first periodic table, then follow the models in order. The neutron came last.

column9: Imagine a gold foil experiment where about HALF of the particles bounced back. What would that suggest about the atom?
column14: The atom is mostly empty space
column15: The atom is packed with dense matter, more like a solid ball
column17: Electrons must travel in fixed orbits
column28: Bouncing back means hitting something dense. If half bounced back, dense matter would fill a large part of the atom, so the atom would NOT be mostly empty space; it would be more like a solid ball. In the real experiment only about 2 in 10,000 bounced back.
column29: In the real experiment, almost nothing bounced back. What did that tell Rutherford?

column9: Leo says, "Bohr proved the Electron Cloud Model was wrong." Which response is best?
column14: He is right; Bohr's fixed orbits replaced the electron cloud.
column15: He is right; the Electron Cloud Model came before the Bohr Model.
column16: He is wrong; the Electron Cloud Model came later and replaced Bohr's fixed orbits.
column17: He is wrong; Bohr and the Electron Cloud Model are the same model.
column28: Leo has the order backwards. The Bohr Model came first (1913). The Electron Cloud Model (1926) came later and replaced Bohr's fixed orbits with shells that have no fixed orbits.
column29: Which model came first, and which one replaced the other?

column9: Which statements about how the atomic model developed are supported by the timeline? Select all that apply.
column14: Each new model came from new evidence or new ideas
column15: Some ideas from older models were kept
column16: Every scientist started over with no help from earlier work
column17: The model changed more than once in the early 1900s
column18: Once a model is proposed, it is never changed
column28: Each model came from new evidence or ideas, some old ideas were kept (like the nucleus), and the model changed several times in the early 1900s (1904, 1911, 1913, 1926). Scientists built on earlier work, and models do change.
column29: Think about the nucleus, the years 1904 to 1926, and whether anyone started from nothing.

column9: Which change in the model moved the positive charge from being spread out to being packed in one small spot?
column28: In the Plum Pudding Model the positive charge was spread through the whole sphere. Rutherford's Nuclear Model packed the positive charge (and the mass) into a small, dense nucleus.
column29: In which model was the positive charge spread out? Which model replaced it?
